This site brings together resources developed for the I-X AI in Science Fellowship, alongside selected external material for scientists and engineers using AI in their research.

The repository includes practical notebooks, slides, recorded sessions, event materials and curated learning pathways. Content is updated as new sessions and resources become available.

Getting started

  • Looking for practical notebooks? Browse the Programming Club.
  • Setting up a GPU job? Visit the HPC resources.
Contributing

Contributions from I-X fellows are welcome. Resources are maintained in the associated GitHub repository and published automatically to this website.

docs.title: Resources developed from the Schmidt AI in Science Fellowship
docs.text:
The following resources emerged from various workshops and conferences led and organized by the Schmidt AI in Science Fellows.

  • Foundation Model for Science Workshop (2025, U Toronto): Tutorials are in the context of protein language models.

  • Symbolic Model Discovery from Time-Series Data (2025, Imperial College London): Lecture recordings and tutorials on PySR and PySINDy.

  • Knowledge-Guided Machine Learning (2025, U Michigan)

  • Pre-workshop materials (sample data and notebooks)

  • Keynote talks

  • Tutorials

  • Ten simple rules for navigating AI in science (2025)

  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Copilot for Scientific Software (2025): Tutorial on building an LLM-powered, domain-specific Q&A chatbot using RAG. This tutorial was offered for the Schmidt AI in Science Postdoctoral Fellows by the eScience Institute at the University of Washington. A video recording is also available.

  • EcoViz (2024, UC San Diego): “A geospatial hub for multidimensional visualizations and data storytelling about impacts to ecosystems and nature-based solutions. From animal behavior to natural flood protection, we showcase biological resilience as a source for hope amidst global change.”

docs.title: Books
docs.text:
• Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning by Christopher M. Bishop. This book is a great introduction to various machine learning methods, it is aimed at advanced undergraduates or first-year PhD students, as well as researchers and practitioners, and assumes no previous knowledge of pattern recognition or machine learning.

  • Deep Learning by I. Goodfellow, Y. Bengio and A. Courville. Authored by pioneers in the field, freely available. Probably the best book on Deep Learning.

  • Dive into Deep Learning by Aston Zhang et al. This book includes coding tutorials and samples.

  • Deep Learning, Foundations and Concepts by Bishop and Bishop. Provides an exhaustive overview of the topic. Accessible to beginners but includes material for advanced learners.

docs.title: Online Courses
docs.text:
• Supervised Machine Learning: Regression and Classification by Andrew Ng. This is a great introduction course on supervised machine learning. The various models/algorithms are first introduced and then applied using Python.

  • Unsupervised Learning, Recommenders, Reinforcement Learning by Andrew Ng. This is a great follow-up to the course above. This course introduces (and applies using Python) various unsupervised machine learning models/algorithms.

  • Deep Learning Specialization by Andrew Ng This is a 5-part specialisation course that introduces (and applies using Python) various deep learning models, from a simple Neural Network to more advanced Recurrent Neural Networks.

  • Practical Deep Learning for Coders from fastai. Associated textbook (“Deep Learning for Coders with fastai & PyTorch: AI Applications without a PhD”).

  • The University of Tübingen ML YouTube channel.

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text:
• Insightful introductions to topics in Deep Learning can also be found at https://distill.pub/.

  • The notebooks by UvA DL are a great introduction to a broad set of topics within ML.

docs.title: Books
docs.text:
• Statistical Rethinking: A Bayesian Course with Examples in R and Stan by Richard McElreath. This is a great introduction to Bayesian statistics for both PhD students and seasoned professionals in the natural and social sciences, and it prepares them for more advanced or specialised statistical modeling. The author provides additional resources, which include online lectures, R code, and Python code.

  • Bayesian Data Analysis by Andrew Gelman, John B. Carlin, Hal S. Stern, and Donald B. Rubin. This book covers a wide range of topics in Bayesian statistics, from single-parameter estimation to non-parametric priors. Additional supporting resources include lectures and code in R, Python, and MATLAB.

  • The Elements of Statistical Learning by Jerome H. Friedman, Robert Tibshirani, and Trevor Hastie. This book covers a wide range of topics in both statistics and machine learning. The book is aimed at people who are interested in “learning from data”.

  • A Student’s Guide to Bayesian Statistics by B Lambert

docs.title: Online Courses
docs.text:
• Statistics and Probability by Khan Academy An excellent introduction to Statistics and Probability aimed at high school students. The course covers a wide range of useful topics, such as hypothesis testing.

  • Statistical Rethinking by Richard McElreath. The course gives a comprehensive and easily accessible introduction to Bayesian statistics. See also the list of books above.

  • Bayesian Statistics Specialization by Herbert Lee from the Coursera learning platform. An excellent 5-part specialisation course which introduces and applies (using R) Bayesian data analytics. The course starts with basic concepts, such as selection priors, and moves on to more advanced topics, such as hierarchical models.

docs.title: Books
docs.text:
• Think Python: How to Think Like a Computer Scientist, 2nd Edition by Allen Downey. This book is a great introduction to computing science using Python. It assumes zero knowledge of Python.

  • Machine Learning from Scratch: Derivations in Concept and Code by Danny Friedman. This is an excellent book that teaches Python by applying machine learning models. The book first introduces the mathematics behind the machine learning models, followed by the Python implementation of the model. The entire book is a Jupyter notebook, and one can download the material.

  • Hands-On Programming with R by Garrett Grolemund. This book is a nice introduction to R programming for non-programmers. It assumes zero knowledge of R.

  • Hands-On Machine Learning with R by Bradley Boehmke & Brandon Greenwell. This is an excellent book which teaches R by applying machine learning models. The book first introduces the mathematics behind the machine learning models, followed by the R implementation of the model.

docs.title: Online Courses
docs.text:
• Applied Software Engineering Fundamentals Specialization by Rav Ahuja. This 5-part specialisation course covers a variety of topics within software engineering, including Shell scripting, Git, and Python. It assumes zero knowledge of programming.

  • Crash Course on Python by Google. This course is great for those who are interested in learning only Python. Like the above course, it assumes zero prior knowledge of programming.

  • Python for Data Science and Machine Learning by Jose Portilla. This course starts from the absolute basics in Python (assumes no prior programming experience).

  • Deep Neural Networks with PyTorch by Joseph Santarcangelo This course introduces PyTorch (a Python library) by demonstrating how to implement deep learning models.

  • Introduction to TensorFlow for Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning by Laurence Moroney. This course introduces TensorFlow (a Python library) by demonstrating how to implement deep learning models.

  • Data Analysis with R Programming by Google. This course is great for those who are interested in learning only R. The course assumes zero prior knowledge.

  • Introduction to Big Data with Spark and Hadoop by Karthik Muthuraman. This is a great course for those interested in learning big data storage.

  • For those who are new to programming tools and want a concise, hands-on introduction, LinkedIn Learning can be very valuable. Imperial College London provides free access to this. LinkedIn Learning also offers courses on career development.

  • Deep Learning Basics by Master Year 2 Data Science from Institut Polytechnique de Paris

  • CS50’s Introduction to Artificial Intelligence with Python by Harvard University. 7-week introductory course.

  • 6.0001 Introduction to Computer Science and Programming in Python from MIT

docs.title: Math Foundation for AI/ML
docs.text:
• Mathematics for Machine Learning: Covers mathematical foundations and example machine learning algorithms that use these mathematical foundations. Free PDF.

  • Mathematical Foundations of Machine Learning: Online course covering linear algebra, calculus, and hands-on lessons in NumPy, TensorFlow, and PyTorch.

docs.title: Linear Algebra
docs.text:
• Linear Algebra by Gilbert Strang. A comprehensive introduction for beginners.

  • Linear Algebra by MathTheBeautiful. YouTube series on linear algebra for absolute beginners.

  • Essence of linear algebra by 3Blue1Brown. YouTube series that goes over basic concepts with animations (geared toward beginners). Recommended for conceptual and visual understanding. Also check out a series on Differential equations, the Essence of calculus, and Neural networks (includes an intro to transformers).

docs.title: Optimisation
docs.text:
• Convex Optimization I and Convex Optimization II by S. Boyd: Great content all over! Lectures 13-19 of COI and all COII are great and generally underrated. An online book is also available.

  • Numerical Optimal Control by M. Diehl and S. Gros: A great source on how to solve OC problems numerically, goes very well with his online course.

  • Nonlinear and Dynamic Optimization: From Theory to Practice by B. Chachuat: This is a great source for a formal and complete description of dynamic optimization problems in engineering practice. It may be more mathematically demanding than the three previous sources.

docs.title: Information theory
docs.text: • Information Theory, Pattern Recognition, and Neural Networks by David MacKay. A classical lecture series that uses information theory to introduce various models/algorithms. The entire lecture series is based on the book.

docs.title: Graph Theory
docs.text: • Introduction to Graph Theory by Robin J. Wilson. A comprehensive and easily accessible book, introducing all the relevant terms for the practitioner.

docs.title: Computer Vision

docs.title: Signal Processing

docs.title: Developing and articulating your research vision
docs.text:
Thursday 1 October 2026, 15:00–17:00 · I-X Conference Room Thursday 22 October 2026 · I-X Conference Room Delivered by: Tracy Bussoli

Fellowship and lectureship opportunities require applicants to communicate a compelling vision for their research. This two-hour session gives you space to step back from day-to-day work, consider where you want to take your research over the next five years, and test your ideas with other fellows.

Through supportive questions and discussion, participants will help one another think creatively and ambitiously about their future research plans.

You will leave with: a written first draft of your research vision.

docs.title: Week 1 (19th May 2026) - Chapter 1: Introduction to Information Theory
docs.text:
• Discussed the format of the book club - shared document for adding questions.
  • "There are no unknown perfect codes over finite fields" [Tietavainen, SIAM J. Appl. Math., Vol. 40, No. 1, Jan. 1973].

docs.title: Week 2 (26th May 2026) - Chapter 2: Probability, Entropy and Inference
docs.text:
• Remind me of Integrated Information Theory (IIT) as a topic which could be interesting for the cohort as an attempt to provide a quantitative description of consciousness which then has application to philosophy of AI. An interesting point for me is: "different physical systems with different internal causal structure may perform the same input-output functions."
  • "One of the themes of this book is that data compression and data modelling are one and the same, and that they should both be addressed ... using inverse probability."
  • Proof of Gibbs' inequality shows that the result is true if you replace $-\log$ with any other convex function, and it turns out there is an appropriate zoo of such things: f-divergences.

docs.title: Week 3 (2nd June 2026) - Chapter 4: The Source Coding Theorem
docs.text:
• "The Shannon information content makes sense: it measures the length of a binary file that encodes x."
  • The "optimum strategy is one that maximises expected information (i.e. entropy) at each choice" is one I have seen applied to Wordle. This is perhaps not important but a bit of fun in a game that does not feel arbitrary.
  • It might be an interesting thought exercise to consider the information required for an (L)LM to work. Predicting the next token with no context is very hard, but context gives information. For example, consider a simple model where tokens are letters and one is predicting the next letter in a name, as in the Wenglish example. $(1/26)^5$ is low compared to $1/32786$, and after two tokens one may have an even better chance of predicting. How should we formalise this intuition?
  • I found the proof of the source coding theorem very unintuitive. Does anyone have insight here?
  • https://scienceline.org/2006/07/tech-schrock-20q/

docs.title: Week 4 (9th June 2026) - Chapter 5: Symbol Codes
docs.text:
• Imagine solving the optimal symbol code problem using Lagrange multipliers, that is minimise $\sum p_i l_i$ such that $\sum 2^{-l_i} = 1$. This works without dealing with discrete code lengths. Should we be concerned? The proof of Theorem 5.1 just takes the ceiling, but comments that these may not give optimal.
  • The Kraft inequality for binary codes can presumably be generalised to the condition $\sum n^{-l_i} \leq 1$ for alphabets of size $n$ by considering that you can encode an alphabet of size $n$ with binary codewords of length $\log_2(n)$.
  • How do we prove that bisecting subsets gives rise to $L(C, X) \leq H(X) + 2$? I cannot get this.
  • https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/questions/8314/comparing-shannon-fano-and-shannon-coding

docs.title: Week 5 (16th June 2026) - Chapter 6: Stream Codes
docs.text:
• Exercise 6.1 provides the answer to the bisecting subset question.
  • The "big picture" makes the point clearly - exponential improvements in encoding cost for a given fixed-length sequence, but also flexibility as the input stream comes in.
  • Laplace's rule and other methods of "additive smoothing" using pseudocounts is on my mind at the moment in terms of answering the question: "what model of smoothing should be used?"
  • The comment on efficient data-entry devices makes me think of an old idea: navigating Google Maps is similar to finding geodesics in hyperbolic space. To go from one place to another we zoom out from the start until both points are visible, then zoom in on the second. Presumably an efficient way of encoding important points on the map is given by how much one needs to zoom in on them to fix them directly.
  • The discussion about where LZ compression fails is very enlightening, with the comment about the use of AI being relevant for this cohort. In the simple case of Fig. 6.11, just "transposing" the image would greatly improve compression. Perhaps we view this as an example of where one learns a representation of data where existing high-performance coding algorithms achieve their best rates.
  • Playing around with this LZ compression can lead one to think of fun ways to waste time, e.g. how would it compress https://oeis.org/A008836 and how does this relate to the Riemann hypothesis?

docs.title: Covariation¶
docs.text: If variation describes the behavior within a variable, covariation describes the behavior between variables. Covariation is the tendency for the values of two or more variables to vary together in a related way. The best way to spot covariation is to visualize the relationship between two or more variables.

docs.title: Introduction to Seaborn for plotting¶
docs.text: Seaborn is a statistical visualisation library, that will make it very easy to visualise categorical/numerical relationships.

At it's simplest, a graph $G$ is a set of vertices (also called nodes) $V$ and edges between these vertices $E$. We visualise them as above, with vertices represented by a point, and edges represented as lines between points.

Note how in the above each vertex gets a label $v$ (here the nonnegative integers) and an edge gets a label $(v, w)$ where $v,w$ are labels of the vertices joined by an edge. In an undirected graph we do not care about the ordering of the vertex labels in an edge, but in a directed graph (or digraph). A graph is simple if it has at most a single edge between any pair of vertices and it has no loops (edges from a vertex to iself). networkx calls a graph that is not simple a MultiGraph. We can also decorate edges with any dictionary of attributes: most commonly one assigns a weight (more later).

We can also define the degree of a vertex to be the number of edges incident to it (for a directed graph one can talk of the in degree and out degree).

You can look at the networkx MultiGraph class to get a sense of what basic properties are available.

We have already seen one representation of a graph, its adjacency matrix $A = A(G)$. For a multidigraph, choosing an ordering of the vertices the entry $A_{ij}$ is the number of edges $i \to j$.

Clearly if $G$ is a simple undirected graph then $A$ is a symmetric binary matrix with zeros on the diagonal. In this case the adjacency matrix is an inefficient way to store the information of the graph $G$. Moreover, if a graph is sparse, that is many entries of adjacency matrix are zero, then this representation is even more inefficient.

That said, with simple undirected graphs the adjacency matrix allows us to perform some magic, for example $$ (A^l)_{ij} = \lvert \text{length-$l$ paths from $i$ to $j$} \rvert. $$

An obvious point to make is that the choice of ordering of the vertices affects $A$, and permutating the vertices corresponds to conjugating $A$ by the associated permutation matrix.

We can also describe graphs as "dicts of dicts of dicts" which is more efficient for large sparse networks. The keys are the vertices (which can thus be given any hashable label), and the corresponding values are themselves dictionaries describing the adjacency data of the vertex (i.e. what it shares an edge with and properties of that edge). Multigraphs go one depth of dictionary further.

A path between two vertices $v, w \in V(G)$ is a collection of vertices $v = v_0, \dots, v_n = w$ (all $v_i$ distinct) such that each of the edges $(v_i, v_{i+1}) \in E$. We think of walking along the edges in the graph from $v$ to $w$. We say a graph is (path) connected if between every pair of edges there is a path. Disconnected graphs correspond to those whose adjacency matrix is, up to some permutation, block diagonal.

A tree is a graph where between any two vertices there exists exactly one path (equivalently a connected acyclic undirected graph). Trees are an extremely useful concept to have clear in your mind because their structure can often give considerable performance improvement to algorithms ($O(n) \to O(\log n)$). They arise in cocepts such as decision tree learning, hierarchical clustering,

We say that two graphs are isomorphic if there is a way to relabel their vertices such there is a 1-1 correspondence between their edges. One can create isomorphic graphs easily by acting with a permutation upon the vertices of one, but in general telling if two graphs are isomorphic is hard. In our present example, entires of the adjacency matrix were a count of edges in a Multigraph. In this perspective, all edges are created equal.

In practice one may wish to have varying weights for edges, which could model

  • resistivity in an electric circuit (electrical engineering)
  • travel time along a route (logistics)
  • proximity (when modelling DNA)

and much more.

To create such simple graphs with weighted edges we can just replace the values in the adjacency matrix with the weights of the edges.

docs.title: Graphs¶
docs.text:
By Linden Disney-Hogg

In the following notebooks, we will delve into the topic of graph neural networks. But to do so, we first have to understand the data that GNNs deal with. So, what are graphs?

Here, we will cover some of the basics, including essential terminology and Python toolkits. For an easy-to-read deep dive into graph theory, I recommend the book Introduction to Graph Theory by Robin J. Wilson.

The essential Python library needed for dealing with graph data is networkx. You can find more tutorials on their homepage.

Before getting going let's make an incomplete list of areas where graphs arise in the 'real' world (can you think of how they appear in your field):

  • logistics (route planning)
  • social networks (identifying cliques, influence)
  • computer science (page ranking, traffic routing, dependency graphs)
  • chemistry (compund structure identification, e.g. alkanes as trees)
  • biology (DNA and protein structure)
  • mathematics (simplicial complexes, dynkin diagrams, tropical curves)
  • linguistics (semantic networks, e.g. for bias analysis)
  • physics (Feynmann diagrams)

I asked ChatGPT to read everyone's research expertise and describe how graph theory applies to their work, perhaps you are included and did not expect it? See the appendix for that output.

As they have been a subject of intense study over many centuries, there are often exceptionally efficient algorithms for computing with graphs: if you can frame a problem you have as a graph problem, you will likely have luck in solving it (at least heuristically) rather efficiently.

As a first example, let's look at the famous problem which kicked off the study of graph theory in 1736: the Königsberg bridge problem. Looking at the map below, can we visit every part of the town crossing each bridge exactly once? Euler turned the problem into one in graph theory, and proved that such a path exists iff the degree of each vertex in the graph is even. We will define these terms and more soon, but first we just use networkx to construct and view the graph.

def evolve(population, f, mutation_rate):
    # selection
    parents = selection(population, f)

    # crossover
    children = []
    for i in range(1, len(parents), 2):
        x1, x2, _ = crossover(parents[i - 1], parents[i])
        children.append(x1)
        children.append(x2)
    children = np.array(children, dtype=np.uint8)

    population = np.vstack([parents, children])

    # mutation
    population = mutate(population, mutation_rate)
    return population

class BinaryGeneticAlgorithm:
    def __init__(self, n_population, dim, mutation_rate, func):
        self.n = n_population
        self.d = dim
        self.mutation_rate = mutation_rate
        self.f = func

        self.population = self.random_population()

    def random_population(self):
        """
        Randomly initialise the population.
        """
        return np.random.randint(
            0, 2, size=(self.n,self.d), dtype=np.uint8
        )

    def evaluate(self, population):
        """
        Evaluate f(x) for the population.
        """
        return np.array([self.f(x) for x in population])

    def selection(self, population, scores):
        """
        Return best half of the population.
        """
        order = np.argsort(scores)
        return population[order[:self.n // 2]].copy()

    def crossover(self, parents):
        """
        Pair up parents and create two children from each pair
        using one-point crossover.
        """
        children = []

        for i in range(0, len(parents) - 1, 2):
            x1 = parents[i]
            x2 = parents[i + 1]

            start, end = sorted(np.random.choice(n, size=2, replace=False))
            end = end + 1

            y1 = np.concatenate([x1[:start], x2[start:end] ,x1[end:]])
            y2 = np.concatenate([x2[:start], x1[start:end] ,x2[end:]])

            children.append(y1.copy())
            children.append(y2.copy())

        return np.array(children, dtype=np.uint8)

    def mutation(self, population):
        """
        Flip bits independently with probability mutation_rate.
        """
        mutated = population.copy()

        mask = np.random.random(size=mutated.shape) < self.mutation_rate
        mutated[mask] = 1 - mutated[mask]

        return mutated

    def evolve(self):
        """
        Run one generation.
        """
        scores = self.evaluate(self.population)

        parents = self.selection(self.population, scores)
        children = self.crossover(parents)

        new_population = np.vstack([parents, children])
        new_population = new_population[:self.n]

        self.population = self.mutation(new_population)

        return self.population

def evolve(population, nodes, mutation_rate):
    """
    Run one generation.
    """
    costs = [cost(x, nodes) for x in population]
    order = np.argsort(costs)

    new_population = []

    # keep best two individuals - no mutation
    for i in range(2):
        new_population.append(population[order[i]].copy())

    # select parents
    parents = population[order[:population.shape[0] // 2]]

    # Create children until population is full
    while len(new_population) < population.shape[0]:
        np.random.shuffle(parents)
        children = crossover(parents)

        for child in children:
            child = mutate(child, mutation_rate)
            new_population.append(child)

            if len(new_population) == population.shape[0]:
                break

    return np.array(new_population)

docs.title: Introduction to Genetic Algorithms¶
docs.text:
by Alex Glyn-Davies

This is a programming club session introducing genetic algorithms. We will cover the following:

  1. What are genetic algorithms? When / why do we use them?
  2. Intro to binary genetic algorithm and genetic operations
  3. Binary genetic algorithm for a toy problem
  4. Travelling Salesman Problem

docs.title: 1. What are genetic algorithms?¶
docs.text:
• Genetic Algorithms (GA) are a class of optimisation methods

general optimisation problem: $$ x\in \mathcal{X}, \quad \text{minimise}\; f(x) $$

  • Inspired by the process of natural selection
  • GA evolve a population of inputs $\{x^{(1)}, \dots, x^{(n)}\}$
  • Select only the most fit individuals to reproduce
  • Fitness is measured by how well the individual minimises $f$

docs.title: Why use genetic algorithms?¶
docs.text:
Optimisation can difficult problem for several reasons.

  • Cost is expensive to evaluate - e.g. computationally expensive simulation, physical experiments..
  • Multimodality - gradient-based methods get stuck in local minima
  • Limited information from $f$ - we may not have access to gradients $\nabla f$

those that use Bayesian Optimisation (BO) have heard this all before... however, BO may be difficult

  • High-dimensionality / Combinatorial spaces: inputs $x$ contain many variables --> search space $\mathcal{X}$ is huge
  • Binary / Categorical input variables

E.g. designing a sequence of 200 base pairs: $ x\in \{A, C, G, T\}^{200} $ to search this space exhaustively would require $\approx 10^{120}$ evaluations of $f$...

docs.title: 2. Binary Genetic Algorithm¶
docs.text: Here we implement a simple binary genetic algorithm. Binary genetic algorithms evolve a population of fixed-length binary variables - these could represent turning on/off parameters in experimental setups, choices in feature selection methods, or could directly code for continuous variables. Population is initially generated at random.

docs.text:
This is a classic problem in computer science.

Given a number of cities and pairwise distances between them, we wish find the path that visits all nodes, returning to the first node, with the shortest possible distance. We will call a path that visits all nodes once and returns to start a tour.

def evolve(population, nodes, mutation_rate):
    """
    Run one generation.
    """
    costs = [cost(x, nodes) for x in population]
    order = np.argsort(costs)

    new_population = []

    # keep best two individuals - no mutation
    for i in range(2):
        new_population.append(population[order[i]].copy())

    # select parents
    parents = population[order[:population.shape[0] // 2]]

    # Create children until population is full
    while len(new_population) < population.shape[0]:
        np.random.shuffle(parents)
        children = crossover(parents)

        for child in children:
            child = mutate(child, mutation_rate)
            new_population.append(child)

            if len(new_population) == population.shape[0]:
                break

    return np.array(new_population)

def torch_gaussian_mi(x, z):
    """
    Differentiable Gaussian Mutual Information estimator using PyTorch.
    Uses log-determinant directly for numerical stability (avoids det() underflow).
    I(X;Z) = 0.5 * [logdet(Cov_X) + logdet(Cov_Z) - logdet(Cov_XZ)]
    """
    joint = torch.cat((x, z), dim=1)

    def get_log_det_cov(data):
        n = data.size(0)
        data_centered = data - data.mean(dim=0)
        cov = (data_centered.t() @ data_centered) / (n - 1)
        # Regularise for numerical stability
        cov = cov + torch.eye(cov.size(0), dtype=data.dtype) * 1e-5
        return torch.logdet(cov)

    log_det_joint = get_log_det_cov(joint)
    log_det_x     = get_log_det_cov(x)
    log_det_z     = get_log_det_cov(z)

    mi = 0.5 * (log_det_x + log_det_z - log_det_joint)
    return mi

def ib_loss_function(y, x, z, beta=0.01):
    """
    IB Loss = beta * I(X; Z) - I(Y; Z)
    z is the bottleneck representation learned by the network.
    X is the input data and Y is the output.
    """
    mi_xz = torch_gaussian_mi(x, z)
    mi_yz = torch_gaussian_mi(y, z)
    # TODO: maximize I(Y;Z) while minimizing I(X;Z)
    total_loss = beta * mi_xz - mi_yz
    return total_loss, mi_xz, mi_yz

        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.hidden.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)
        opt_enc.step()

    # ── Phase 2: Freeze encoder, train decoder with MSE ──────────────────────
    for p in model.hidden.parameters():
        p.requires_grad = False

    opt_dec = optim.SGD(model.output.parameters(), lr=0.01)
    model.output.train()

    for epoch in range(phase2_epochs):
        opt_dec.zero_grad()
        with torch.no_grad():
            z = model.hidden(X_train)
        y_hat = model.output(z)
        loss = criterion(y_hat, y_train)
        loss.backward()
        opt_dec.step()

    # ── Evaluation ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

    with torch.no_grad():

        train_mse = criterion(y_train_hat, y_train).item()

docs.title: Information, Invariance and Generalisation¶
docs.text:
by Hardik Rajpal

This notebook explores the fundamental concepts of Information Theory and how they extend to the Information Bottle framework in Deep Learning to enable robust generalisation.

docs.title: 1. What is information?¶
docs.text:
Information is defined as the 'surprise' of an event. For a given event with probability $p_i$, the information is: $$I(p_i) = -\log(p_i)$$

Shannon entropy is the average information across all possible outcomes: $$H = -\sum_{i} p_i \log(p_i)$$

docs.title: 2. Mutual Information¶
docs.text: Mutual Information (MI) measures how much information is shared between two variables. Unlike Pearson correlation, which only detects linear relationships, MI can capture non-linear interdependencies.

docs.title: Linear vs. Non-linear mappings¶
docs.text: We will compare how MI and Pearson correlation behave when we introduce a dependency between two binary sequences $x$ and $y$ controlled by a probability $p$.

docs.title: 2.1 Implementing Mutual Information¶
docs.text:
The Mutual Information between two discrete variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as: $$I(X;Y) = \sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} \sum_{y \in \mathcal{Y}} p(x,y) \log\left( \frac{p(x,y)}{p(x)p(y)} \right)$$

Where:

  • $p(x,y)$ is the joint probability distribution of $X$ and $Y$.
  • $p(x)$ and $p(y)$ are the marginal probability distributions of $X$ and $Y$ respectively.

docs.title: 2.2 Comparing Mappings¶
docs.text:
We will now compare two types of dependencies:

  1. Linear Mapping: $y$ simply copies binary $x$ with probability $p$.
  2. Non-linear (Quadratic): Here $x$ can take three values (-1, 0, 1). $y$ is defined as the $y = x^2$.

docs.title: 2.3 Continuous Mutual Information: Gaussian Case¶
docs.text:
When dealing with continuous variables, calculating MI can be more complex. However, if two variables $X$ and $Y$ follow a joint Multivariate Gaussian distribution, the Mutual Information can be calculated analytically using their covariance matrix $\Sigma$.

The formula for Gaussian Mutual Information is: $$I(X; Y) = \frac{1}{2} \ln \left( \frac{|\Sigma_{XX}| |\Sigma_{YY}|}{|\Sigma|} \right)$$

Where:

  • $|\Sigma|$ is the determinant of the joint covariance matrix.
  • $|\Sigma_{XX}|$ and $|\Sigma_{YY}|$ are the determinants of the marginal covariance matrices.

docs.title: 3. Information Bottleneck¶
docs.text:
The Information Bottleneck (IB) principle provides a framework for understanding how deep learning models extract useful features. Given an input $X$, a target output $Y$, and a learned representation (or latent code) $Z$, we want to find a representation $Z$ that is as concise as possible while still being highly predictive of $Y$.

This is formulated as an optimization problem where we minimize the IB objective function: $$\mathcal{L} = \beta I(X; Z) - I(Y; Z)$$

Where:

  • $I(X; Z)$: The information the representation $Z$ retains about the input $X$. Minimizing this encourages compression and the removal of irrelevant noise.
  • $I(Y; Z)$: The information the representation $Z$ contains about the target $Y$. Maximizing this ensures the representation is useful for the task.
  • $\beta$: A trade-off parameter (Lagrange multiplier) that controls the balance between compression and task accuracy.

By constraining $Z$ to be low-dimensional (a "bottleneck"), we force the model to capture the invariant features—the underlying patterns that are necessary for generalisation while ignoring superficial fluctuations in the input data.

docs.title: Exercise: Nuisance Signals and Invariance¶
docs.text: In this exercise we investigate how the IB penalty helps a model ignore 'nuisance' signals — input features that are correlated with the target during training but uninformative at test time.

docs.title: The Data Setup¶
docs.text:
We define a 3D input $X = [a, b, c]$ and a scalar target $Y = a + b$:

Variable Distribution Role $a \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$ signal component 1 contributes to $Y$ $b \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$ signal component 2 contributes to $Y$ $c_\text{train} = (a+b) + \mathcal{N}(0, 0.05)$ near-perfect proxy for $Y$ during training gradient descent will greedily use $c$ $c_\text{test} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$ independent noise at test time any reliance on $c$ gives high test MSE

This train/test distribution shift on $c$ is the setup that makes IB useful. Without the IB penalty the model exploits the shortcut $c \approx Y$. The IB penalty forces it to compress $Z$ until only the true signal $(a, b)$ survives.

docs.title: Model Architecture (3 → 2 → 1)¶
docs.text:
Both models share the same architecture — a linear encoder projecting the 3D input to a 2D bottleneck $Z$, followed by a linear decoder:

$$Z = W_\text{enc} \cdot [a, b, c]^\top \qquad \hat{Y} = w_\text{dec} \cdot Z$$

The 2D bottleneck is narrower than the 3D input, forcing the encoder to compress. The key question is which input dimensions survive.

docs.title: Comparison: MSE vs. IB Training¶
docs.text:
Case 1 — MSE Only: trained end-to-end to minimise $\text{MSE}(Y, \hat{Y})$. Gradient descent exploits $c$ because it nearly perfectly predicts $Y$ during training, which fails at test time.

Case 2 — Information Bottleneck (two-phase training):

  • Phase 1 trains only the encoder with the IB objective $\beta \cdot I(X;Z) - I(Y;Z)$. The $-I(Y;Z)$ term pushes the encoder toward dimensions informative about $Y$; $+\beta \cdot I(X;Z)$ penalises encoding the full input, discouraging reliance on the nuisance $c$.
  • Phase 2 freezes the encoder and trains only the decoder with MSE — a linear readout on top of the fixed representation.

By sweeping $\beta$ we trace the IB trade-off: small $\beta$ still uses the shortcut; optimal $\beta$ suppresses the nuisance $(\|w_c\| \to 0)$ and minimises test MSE; large $\beta$ over-compresses and degrades performance.

docs.title: 3.1 Case 1: MSE Only Loss¶
docs.text: In this baseline case, we train the model to minimize the standard Mean Squared Error. We will monitor the latent representation $Z$ to see if the model naturally ignores the nuisance signal $c$.

docs.title: 4.2 Case 2: Information Bottleneck (IB) Loss¶
docs.text:
We train this model in two separate phases, keeping the encoder and decoder objectives clean and non-conflicting.

Phase 1 — Learn the representation (100 epochs, encoder only):

$$\mathcal{L}_\text{enc} = \beta \cdot I(X; Z) - I(Y; Z)$$

  • $-I(Y;Z)$: maximise the information the bottleneck retains about the target $Y$. This term is direction-sensitive — its gradient depends on how well $Z$ predicts $Y$, so it pushes the encoder toward the true signal $s$
  • $+\beta \cdot I(X;Z)$: compression penalty — penalise retaining any information about the full input $X$, discouraging the encoder from encoding the nuisance $c$

Only the encoder weights are updated in this phase. The decoder is untouched.

Phase 2 — Fit the decoder (100 epochs, decoder only, encoder frozen):

$$\mathcal{L}_\text{dec} = \text{MSE}(Y, \hat{Y})$$

The encoder weights are frozen. A linear decoder is trained by simple regression on top of the fixed representation $Z$. This cleanly separates what is encoded from how it is decoded.

To calculate $I(X;Z)$ and $I(Y;Z)$ during Phase 1, we use the differentiable Gaussian MI estimator from Section 2.3.
